exercises.title: Who defines what
lesson: Three parties each write a different part of tool use.

Anthropic defines the envelope: a response has `content` blocks; a tool request is a block with `type`, `id`, `name` and `input`; `stop_reason` says why Claude stopped. That shape is the same for every tool anyone ever writes.
You, the developer, define the tools: each tool's `name`, its `description`, and its `input_schema`, which lists the argument names and types. You also write the Python function that does the work.
Claude decides, each turn, whether to ask for a tool, which one, and what values to put in the arguments. It can only use the names and argument keys you declared.
So `balance_id` appears in `block.input` because the definition in `tools` declares it. Nobody at Anthropic chose that key, and Claude did not invent it.
exercises.task: `definition` is what you declared and `request` is what Claude sent back. Replace each `None` by reading from one of them (do not type the values), so that both comparisons print `True`. Then write three short sentences in the explanation box: what Anthropic defines, what you define, and what Claude decides.
exercises.starter:
definition = tools[0]              # written by you, the developer
for block in response.content:     # written by Claude, in Anthropic's format
    if block.type == "tool_use":
        request = block

# Replace each None by reading from `definition` or `request`.
declared_name = None     # the tool name you declared
declared_keys = None     # list of the argument names you declared (the keys of "properties")
requested_name = None    # the tool name Claude asked for
requested_keys = None    # list of the argument names Claude supplied

print(declared_name == requested_name)
print(declared_keys == requested_keys)
tests: declared_name and declared_keys are read from the definition
requested_name and requested_keys are read from the tool_use block
prints True then True for the matching pair
still correct for a different tool; prints False when Claude's keys differ
explanation separates Anthropic, developer and Claude
hints: The definition is a dictionary: `definition["name"]`. The request is an SDK object: `request.name`.
The declared argument names are the keys of `definition["input_schema"]["properties"]`. `list(some_dict)` gives a list of its keys.
`request.input` is a plain dictionary, so `list(request.input)` gives the argument names Claude supplied.

exercises.title: Define a tool with no arguments
lesson: A tool definition is a dictionary with three keys. `name` is what Claude will ask for. `description` is plain English that tells Claude what the tool does and when to use it. `input_schema` describes the arguments.

`input_schema` is always `{"type": "object", "properties": {...}}`. Each entry in `properties` is one argument. An empty `properties` means the tool takes no arguments, which is right when your program already knows which instrument it is connected to.
For such a tool Claude's request arrives with `input` equal to `{}`.

exercises.title: Declare required and optional arguments
lesson: To let Claude choose between several balances, the tool needs an argument. You declare it under `properties`, with a type and preferably a description: `"balance_id": {"type": "string", "description": "..."}`.
`required` is a list of the argument names Claude must always send. Anything in `properties` but not in `required` is optional, and Claude may leave it out.
`"enum": ["g", "mg"]` restricts an argument to the listed values.
This schema is about what goes into the tool. It says nothing about what the tool returns; your Python function decides that.
exercises.task: Complete the definition so that `read_balance` takes `balance_id` (a string, required) and `unit` (a string, optional, one of `g` or `mg`). Give each argument a short `description`.

hints: Each argument is its own small dictionary: `"balance_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Which balance to read"}`.
Add `"required": ["balance_id"]` beside `"properties"`, inside `input_schema`. It is a list, even with one name.
For `unit`, add `"enum": ["g", "mg"]` next to its `"type"`. Leave `unit` out of `required`.

exercises.title: Compare a request with its definition
lesson: Before writing a dispatcher, read the definition: it tells you which keys `block.input` will have. The same request can fit one definition and not another.
Here Claude's request is `read_balance` with `{"balance_id": "XPR205"}`. That fits `id_tool`. It does not fit `no_argument_tool`, which declares no arguments at all.
exercises.task: Complete `check_request(definition, block)` so it returns a list of problems: `"wrong tool"` if the names differ, `"missing <key>"` for each required key absent from `block.input`, and `"unexpected <key>"` for each key in `block.input` that the definition does not declare. A request that fits returns `[]`.
exercises.starter:
def check_request(definition, block):
    problems = []
    schema = definition["input_schema"]
    # 1. block.name must equal the declared name, otherwise add "wrong tool"
    # 2. each key in schema.get("required", []) must be in block.input, otherwise add "missing <key>"
    # 3. each key in block.input must be in schema["properties"], otherwise add "unexpected <key>"
    return problems

for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "tool_use":
        print(check_request(id_tool, block))
        print(check_request(no_argument_tool, block))
tests: the same request against the no-argument definition returns ['unexpected balance_id']
a missing required key is reported; a missing optional key is not
a different tool name is reported as wrong tool
a definition with no required list does not crash
hints: `problems.append("missing " + key)` builds the message for one key.
Loop over `schema.get("required", [])` and test `if key not in block.input`. `.get` matters because `no_argument_tool` has no `required` entry.
For the third rule, loop over `block.input` (its keys) and test `if key not in schema["properties"]`.

story: So far the `if` / `elif` that picks a tool sat inside the loop. Here you move it into a function of its own, so that any part of a program can say: run the tool called this, with these arguments.

`name` is text such as `"read_balance"`. `args` is a dictionary such as `{"balance_id": "XPR205"}`. They are the same two things as `block.name` and `block.input`, but this exercise has no `response` and no loop. You write only the function. Check calls it directly, several times, with different names.

exercises.title: Read imports
lesson: Real programs are spread over several files. `import` is how one file reaches code in another. There are three forms, and you will see all of them at the top of any agent.
`import instruments` brings in the whole file. You reach things inside it with a dot: `instruments.read_balance(...)`.
`from instruments import read_balance` brings in one name. You then call it directly: `read_balance(...)`.
`import instruments as lab` brings in the whole file under a shorter name: `lab.read_balance(...)`.

When you see a name you do not recognise in someone's code, look at the imports first: they tell you which file or library it came from. `import anthropic` and `from anthropic.types import Message` are the same two forms.

Add the other two: import only the function and call it by its own name, then import the module under the name `lab` and call `lab.read_balance`. Each call uses `"XPR205"` and prints its result, so the program prints the same reading three times.

# Three ways to reach the same function in instruments.py.

# 1. Import only the function, then call it by its own name and print the result.

# 2. Import the module under the short name lab, then call lab.read_balance and print the result.
tests: the same reading is printed three times
one import uses from instruments import read_balance
one import uses import instruments as lab
the function is not copied into main.py
hints: Form 2 is one line: `from instruments import read_balance`. After it, `read_balance("XPR205")` works with no prefix.
Form 3 is `import instruments as lab`. After it, `lab` means the same file as `instruments`.
Each of the two needs its own `print(...)` line, as the first form has.

exercises.title: Read a class and self
lesson: A class is a blueprint for objects that carry their own data. `Balance("XPR205")` makes one object; Python runs `__init__` to set it up.
`self` is the object itself. Python fills it in for you, so you always pass one argument fewer than the `def` line shows: `__init__(self, balance_id, unit="g")` is called as `Balance("XPR205")`.
`self.balance_id = balance_id` stores a value on the object. Afterwards `balance.balance_id` reads it. Each object has its own copy.
A function inside a class is a method. `balance.read()` runs `read` with `self` set to that object.

You have used this all along: `client.messages.create(...)` is an object (`client`), an attribute of it that is another object (`messages`), and a method (`create`). `response.content` and `block.name` are attributes.

exercises.title: Read a traceback and catch an exception
lesson: When Python cannot carry on, it raises an exception and prints a traceback. Read a traceback from the bottom up.
The last line is the kind of error and its message: `KeyError: 'sensor'` means a dictionary was asked for the key `sensor` and did not have it.
The pair of lines just above it is where it happened: the file, the line number, the function, and the line of code itself. Higher pairs show who called that function.

`try:` and `except KeyError as exc:` let a program carry on. The code under `try` is attempted; if that kind of error is raised, the code under `except` runs instead, and `exc` holds the error. `raise ValueError("...")` is how code reports a problem of its own.

exercises.title: Read type hints, docstrings and f-strings
lesson: `def format_reading(mass: float, unit: str = "g", places: int = 2) -> str:` looks dense. Take away the hints and it is `def format_reading(mass, unit="g", places=2):`.

`: float`, `: str` and `-> str` are type hints: notes saying what kind of value is expected and what comes back. Python does not check them when the program runs. Editors and some libraries read them; the SDK's `@beta_tool` builds a tool's `input_schema` from them.
`= "g"` is a default: the argument may be left out. Arguments can also be given by name, `places=0`, in any order.
The string in triple quotes straight after the `def` line is a docstring: the function's description for readers and tools.
An f-string, `f"..."`, puts values into text: `f"{name}: {value}"`. After a colon comes a format: `{mass:.2f}` means two decimal places.

exercises.title: Read a decorator
lesson: A line starting with `@` above a `def` is a decorator. `@tool` above `def read_balance():` means: define the function, then pass it to `tool`, and keep whatever `tool` hands back under the same name. It is exactly `read_balance = tool(read_balance)`.
That happens once, when the `def` is reached, not each time the function is called.

Decorators are how libraries let you register things. The `tool` on the left adds each function to the dictionary `TOOLS` under its own name. The SDK's `@beta_tool` does something similar: it reads the function and builds the tool definition from it.
A dictionary can hold functions. `TOOLS["read_balance"]` is the function itself; adding `()` calls it.

exercises.title: Read one-line loops
lesson: Experienced Python writers often fold a loop into one line. `[block.name for block in response.content if block.type == "tool_use"]` is a list comprehension. Read it from the middle: for each block in the content, if it is a tool_use, take its name; the square brackets collect the results into a list.
It is the same as starting with an empty list, looping, testing with `if`, and appending. Nothing more.
With curly brackets and a colon it builds a dictionary instead: `{block.name: block.input for block in ...}`.
`for key, value in some_dict.items():` goes through a dictionary giving you each key together with its value.
`"\n".join(list_of_strings)` glues strings into one, with a new line between them. It is how most agents turn several text blocks into one answer.
exercises.task: The first two lines of the starter are written in the one-line style. Build `names_loop` with an ordinary `for` loop so that it equals `names`. Go through `inputs` with `.items()` and fill `needs` with one string per tool in the form `read_balance: {'balance_id': 'XPR205'}`. Set `answer` to the text of all the text blocks joined with `"\n"`.

inputs = {block.name: block.input for block in response.content if block.type == "tool_use"}

# 1. Build the same list as names with an ordinary for loop.
names_loop = []

# 2. Go through inputs with .items(): one string per tool, like  read_balance: {'balance_id': 'XPR205'}
needs = []

# 3. The text of every text block, joined with "\n".
answer = None

print(names_loop)
print(needs)
print(answer)
tests: names_loop equals names, for any response
needs has one '<name>: <input>' string per requested tool
answer is the text blocks joined with a new line
nothing is typed in: a different response gives different results
hints: `for block in response.content:` then `if block.type == "tool_use":` then `names_loop.append(block.name)`.
`for name, tool_input in inputs.items():` then `needs.append(f"{name}: {tool_input}")`.

exercises.title: A second tool, and tools that fail
exercises.todo: add check_temperature with an argument, and turn every tool failure into an error result
lesson: Real instruments fail, and Claude sometimes asks for something you cannot do. An agent that crashes on the first failure is no use in a lab. Instead, the failure is sent back to Claude as a tool_result with `"is_error": True` and text saying what went wrong. Claude then tells the person.

The pattern is `try:` run the tool, `except Exception as exc:` build the error text. Every tool request must still get a result, whether it worked or not.

exercises.title: Steer the agent with words
exercises.todo: write rules, send them as the system prompt, and improve both tool descriptions
lesson: Two pieces of plain English shape what Claude does: the system prompt and the tool descriptions. Changing them is often the fix for an agent that behaves badly, and it needs no new Python.
The system prompt is a parameter of the request, `system=...`, beside `messages` and `tools`. It is not a message, and like everything else it must be sent with every request.

Write it for a reader who knows nothing but what you say: what the assistant is for, what it must never do, and what to do when something fails. For a lab, the most important rule is that a reading comes from a tool or is not stated at all.
A tool description should say what the tool does, what comes back, and what a failure looks like. Your real balance description already does this.
The simulated Claude only proves that the rules arrive (ask it "who are you?"). To see rules change behaviour, use Run live and try the same questions with and without a rule.
